# Gammon India Limited: Credit-Risk Events and Red Flags, FY2025-26

*Source: Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 (cited as [IAR p.X]). All figures are Rs crore unless stated. Standalone figures are used unless marked "consolidated."*

## Bottom line

The excerpts describe a company in severe, long-running distress. Most bank facilities have been recalled and classified as current liabilities, principal and interest are in default (most for more than 365 days), net worth is deeply negative, both auditor reports carry qualifications and a material going-concern uncertainty, and the stock is suspended. The restructuring that management has relied on for years has not concluded. Recovery depends on outcomes the report itself describes as unresolved.

## 1. Lender actions

- **NPA status:** Facilities have been NPA since June 2017 [IAR p.4, p.110].
- **Recall:** Lenders recalled all facilities. Long-term loans of ₹2,636.59 cr are reclassified as current [IAR p.110, p.117]. Recalled credit facilities total ₹4,053.90 cr (standalone) [IAR p.115].
- **Legal recovery:** Lenders have filed recovery suits in Debt Recovery Tribunals and an insolvency petition at NCLT Mumbai. The secured lenders that filed the petition later withdrew it [IAR p.4].
- **Asset enforcement:** Union Bank of India (assigned to Omkara ARC) and Punjab National Bank (assigned to CFM ARC) have taken possession of the Gammon House property under SARFAESI and restrained the company from parting with its rights in it [IAR p.98]. Lenders also took possession of ACGB in May 2019 and are pursuing e-auction [IAR p.172].
- **Debt sales:** More than 50% of debt has been assigned to two ARCs [IAR p.68]. IDBI, Canara and PNB assigned facilities to CFM [IAR p.79].
- **Pledges:** Promoter shares are pledged, and a personal guarantee from former CMD Abhijit Rajan is held [IAR p.117].
- **Restructuring history:** The company went into CDR, then SDR (lenders obtained about 62% equity in 2015). An Inter-Creditor Agreement followed in 2019 [IAR p.3]. A 2021 resolution plan was approved by some lenders but remains unconcluded because lenders have not reached consensus [IAR p.24, p.205].

## 2. Payment defaults (standalone, as at 31 March 2026)

| Category | Amount | Ageing / note | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Principal default | ₹4,053.90 cr | Most >365 days | IAR p.79 |
| Interest default (term and NCD) | ₹2,820.26 cr | Mixed; most >365 days | IAR p.80 |
| Interest default on short-term facilities (CC, WCDL, STL) | ₹546.90 cr | Part of recalled debt | IAR p.80, p.190 |
| **Total interest default** | **₹3,367.16 cr** | 2,932.23 in >365 days | IAR p.75, p.119 |
| NPA interest accrued in books | ₹3,786.28 cr | | IAR p.115 |
| Debenture redemption reserve shortfall (15% liquid assets) | ₹43.25 cr not set aside | Due to financial crunch | IAR p.86 |

- Winding-up petitions have been filed by various creditors, and the company has been settling some under agreed terms [IAR p.4, p.68].
- The company has not declared the NCD default resolved. It is defaulting on statutory dues, with undisputed dues outstanding [IAR p.73].

## 3. Auditor concerns

**Standalone and consolidated: both qualified.**

- **Going concern (material uncertainty):** Current liabilities exceed current assets by ₹12,701.41 cr [IAR p.68, p.132]. The auditors say the company cannot meet obligations as they fall due and that the matters "may have an adverse effect on the functioning of the Company" [IAR p.70].
- **Penal interest:** The lenders' penal interest is ₹391.76 cr cumulative, plus ₹519.78 cr levied by CFM ARC. The management disputes these and has not booked them. Total unaccounted penal interest is ₹911.54 cr [IAR p.67, p.121]. The auditors cannot say whether a provision is required [IAR p.44].
- **Receivables:** Trade receivables of ₹532.91 cr rely on arbitration awards that the client is challenging in court [IAR p.68]. The CMRL award has been written down and the company's share retained at ₹408 cr [IAR p.102].
- **Claims:** ₹10 cr of claims is retained, which the auditors could not verify [IAR p.67].
- **Title deeds:** Title deeds are held by IDBI Trusteeship and the auditors could not confirm ownership [IAR p.72].
- **Going-concern note for subsidiaries:** The holding company's referral to NCLT means it cannot provide financial support [IAR p.197].
- **Internal controls:** The auditors cannot state that internal financial controls are adequate, citing manpower and liquidity [IAR p.78].
- **Other audit points:** Working capital statements have not been filed with banks since June 2017 [IAR p.72, p.120]. Inventory is held by a client under arbitration and is not confirmed [IAR p.181]. Loans to related parties are about 98.6% of loans given and are largely provided for [IAR p.72, p.178].

## 4. Market and listing fallout

- BSE compulsorily delisted the shares in January 2024, and NSE followed in May 2024 [IAR p.28, p.63].
- The company appealed to SAT. SAT ordered relisting after compliance. The status is now "suspended," not delisted. Trading is suspended and no price data exists [IAR p.59–60].
- The company has completed compliance with BSE, but NSE compliance is still in progress [IAR p.63].

## 5. Governance and compliance

- **Director disqualifications:** Four directors are disqualified under Section 164(2)(b) for NCD default exceeding one year: Kashi Nath Chatterjee, Lily Bhushan, Mahendra Ujamshi Shah and Vishwas Joglekar [IAR p.30, p.65]. Auditors say all directors except two are disqualified [IAR p.70].
- **Remuneration:** Executive remuneration was paid without the lenders' NOC, contrary to Section 197 [IAR p.70].
- **Company Secretary vacancy:** Vacant 16 June to 5 December 2025. Two MGT-14 filings were late by 36 and 52 days [IAR p.28].
- **Late audited results:** FY2024-25 results were approved on 2 August 2025, late under LODR Regulation 33 [IAR p.31].
- **Late ROC filings:** Several e-form filings were late [IAR p.37, p.63].
- **Other:** A Maternity Benefit Act disclosure was omitted [IAR p.28]. Audit trail at application level is retained only from 22 April 2024 [IAR p.71].
- **FEMA and RBI:** The company is compounding FEMA non-compliances, with liability not ascertainable [IAR p.127]. The RBI has directed a refund of ₹16.64 cr share application money (at the Ansaldo subsidiary), which has not been done [IAR p.142, p.197].
- **Possible fraud or control failure:** ₹1.08 cr was remitted to an unauthorised account after a supplier's email was compromised. Legal action is underway [IAR p.203].

## 6. Overseas and subsidiary exposure

- **Campo Puma Oriente S.A.:** Accounts unaudited since December 2012. Exposure is ₹430.19 cr, and a Standby LC was invoked by IDBI Dubai. The company has made a full provision. A partner dispute in Oklahoma is pending [IAR p.127, p.172].
- **Sofinter (Italy):** The group's net worth has eroded by more than two-thirds, requiring a Euro 14 million equity call under Article 2446 of the Italian Civil Code. Nova Energy has undertaken to cover any shortfall [IAR p.24]. The group's consolidated loss was Euro 7.5 million on revenue of Euro 252 million [IAR p.24].
- **Franco Tosi Meccanica:** Fully provided and impaired [IAR p.174].
- **Guarantees:** Corporate guarantees given to bankers total ₹746.35 cr [IAR p.126].
- **Subsidiaries:** Several SPVs and Dutch holding companies have large negative net worth. Some subsidiaries are not audited, and Ansaldo Caldaie's accounts carry qualifications [IAR p.35, p.142].

## 7. Financial position

| Metric | FY2025-26 | FY2024-25 |
|---|---|---|
| Standalone turnover | ₹85.18 cr | ₹21.23 cr |
| Standalone net loss after tax | ₹(1,189.01) cr | ₹(1,078.14) cr |
| Consolidated net loss after tax | ₹(1,170.34) cr | ₹(1,192.34) cr |
| Finance cost (standalone) | ₹1,123.06 cr | ₹1,005.42 cr |
| Standalone total equity | ₹(11,755.05) cr | ₹(10,565.84) cr |
| Consolidated total equity | ₹(13,091.66) cr | ₹(11,533.92) cr |
| Accumulated losses (standalone) | ₹(13,760.87) cr | ₹(12,572.00) cr |

Sources: [IAR p.4, p.22, p.81, p.82, p.212].

Losses are driven mainly by interest and finance cost, which is greater than turnover. The company has ₹20.61 cr of current assets against ₹12,722.02 cr of current liabilities [IAR p.81].

## 8. Management's position and mitigants

Management says the following. None of these is confirmed in the excerpts as completed:

- An OTS proposal has been submitted and is under lender consideration [IAR p.4, p.6].
- ARC has agreed in principle to settle on principal only, waiving interest and penal charges, which management calls "a high possibility" [IAR p.121]. Senior management approval at the ARC is pending.
- A new investor is expected to infuse funds. The earlier investor (Everstone) fell away, and an alternative investor was accepted by bankers in 2022 [IAR p.24].
- The Sofinter stake sale to a new investor for 90% at Euro 12 million is at the share-purchase-agreement stage [IAR p.127].

The auditors describe the resolution plan as dependent on "too many variables" with "no progress" [IAR p.68, p.205].

## 9. Overall assessment

**The situation is very serious.** Based on the excerpts, the company:

- has no realistic near-term ability to service its debt;
- has all bank facilities recalled, most in default for over a year;
- has negative equity of roughly ₹11,755 cr standalone and ₹13,092 cr consolidated;
- has an unconcluded restructuring with lenders split and assets being enforced by ARCs;
- faces qualified audit opinions and a going-concern material uncertainty;
- is suspended from trading, with directors disqualified and governance lapses.

For a legacy exposure, the key recovery questions are:

- whether ARC or lender settlements are concluded, and on what haircut;
- whether the Sofinter and other overseas stakes can be realised;
- whether arbitration awards (₹532.91 cr receivables) survive court challenges;
- whether the ₹911.54 cr penal interest is waived.

The excerpts do not provide a recovery estimate, asset valuation or ranking of creditor claims, so I cannot quantify recoverability.

## 10. Data notes

- Default totals differ across tables, depending on scope (e.g., ₹4,053.90 cr principal default vs ₹2,636.59 cr recalled long-term loans vs ₹5,340.91 cr for holding company and foreign SPVs [IAR p.79, p.117, p.189]). Reconcile before relying on any single figure.
- Provisions and receivables figures for the CMRL award vary between ₹532 cr and ₹408 cr across sections [IAR p.102, p.176].
- The report contains a placeholder "[Year]" in the trading suspension note [IAR p.43].

# Gammon India: Credibility of the Revival Story

**Short answer:** The revival story rests on a lender-approved resolution plan and a proposed one-time settlement (OTS) backed by a new investor. Management is optimistic, but the auditor's report, the balance sheet and the history of stalled approvals do not support that optimism. The settlement sources are mostly contingent: unrealised arbitration awards, a Gammon House property under enforcement, pledged shares, and a potential sale of the Sofinter stake. No firm, committed cash source is identified in the excerpts.

Citations below refer to *Integrated Annual Report 2025-26, Gammon India Limited* (the "Report").

## 1. What the resolution plan is built on

- **Legal framework:** CDR referral in March 2013 [Report p23]; CDR package approved June 2013 and Master Restructuring Agreement signed September 2013 [Report p115]; SDR under which lenders received about 62% equity [Report p3]; an Inter-Creditor Agreement (ICA) executed in 2019 under RBI's 7 June 2019 circular [Report p3].
- **Core mechanism:** Hiving off the main business, which the Report says resolved 75% of lender dues [Report p23]. The residual company's primary task is to "maximize recovery to repay Residual debt" [Report p6].
- **Current proposal:** An OTS proposal submitted at the lenders' request and "under consideration" [Report p4]. Management describes it as "subject to waiver of interest and penal charges and a haircut on the principal outstanding" [Report p68].
- **Investor dependence:** Revival is conditional on the investor infusing further funds [Report p3, p4].

## 2. How the plan has evolved

| Period | Development | Source |
|---|---|---|
| FY2012–13 | Slowdown, project delays, stretched working capital; referral to CDR | Report p23 |
| Jun–Sep 2013 | CDR package approved; MRA executed | Report p115 |
| Nov 2015 | Scheme of corporate realignment and SDR approved | Report p3 |
| June 2017 | Facilities classified as NPA; lenders recall loans | Report p4, p110 |
| 2019 | ICA executed; Deloitte appointed as Process Advisor; Duff & Phelps engaged for valuation | Report p23–24 |
| Post-2019 | Draft plan; seven lenders gave in-principle sanction, but the Everstone investor fund closed due to delay by other bankers | Report p24 |
| 2022 | Alternate investor on the same terms accepted by bankers; Joint Lenders' Meeting 5 March 2022 disagreed on the timeline; plan left unconcluded | Report p24 |
| 2023–2024 | Debt assigned to ARCs: Union Bank to OARPL (2024); IDBI, Canara, PNB to CFM | Report p79–80 |
| FY2025–26 | More than 50% of debt assigned to ARCs; company negotiating waiver and haircut with ARCs | Report p24, p68 |

The Report itself says that "repeated partial approved Resolution process is not serving the purpose" [Report p6].

## 3. Credibility assessment

**Supporting management's view:**
- Some lenders (seven at one stage) gave in-principle sanction [Report p24].
- CFM ARC has considered settling on principal only, waiving interest and penalties, though approval is pending [Report p67, p121].
- Management reports positive discussions with ARCs [Report p68].

**Undermining it:**
- The auditor states that the plan "is dependent on too many variables and on account of there being no progress" [Report p68].
- The auditor reports that lenders "are not able to reach a consensus," with "hardly any progress" [Report p205–206].
- Trading in the equity shares is suspended, and several creditors have filed winding-up petitions [Report p68].
- Current liabilities exceed current assets by Rs 12,701.41 crore at 31 March 2026 [Report p68; p110].
- The company has "severe manpower issues" and is defaulting on statutory obligations [Report p68].
- The holding company is referred to NCLT and "unable to extend any kind of financial support" [Report p197].
- Management itself says that cash flows from projects "could not be materialised" [Report p23].

## 4. What assets or cash sources stand behind any settlement

**Cash position (standalone, 31 March 2026):**
- Total current assets are only Rs 20.61 crore; cash is Rs 0.00 crore and bank balances Rs 2.82 crore, of which some are restricted and need lender approval [Report p81; p108].
- Net cash from operations in FY2025–26 was Rs 6.55 crore [Report p83].
- The auditor notes cash losses of Rs 1,048.68 crore in the current year [Report p75].

**Assets with potential realisable value (all contingent or encumbered):**
- **Arbitration awards and receivables:** Non-current trade receivables are Rs 541.52 crore, mostly disputed awards under appeal by clients [Report p102–103]. Recoverability of Rs 532.91 crore depends on the outcome of appeals [Report p68]. Realisation "continues to remain a big challenge" [Report p4]. The CMRL award was reduced to Rs 408 crore [Report p102].
- **Gammon House:** Banks have taken over possession of the property under SARFAESI, and the company is restrained from parting with rights [Report p98]. It is subject to first and second charges in favour of lenders [Report p116–118].
- **Fixed assets:** Net block is Rs 401.57 crore, of which freehold property is Rs 393.14 crore [Report p98].
- **Subsidiary investments:** Investments in impaired subsidiaries (Rs 1,536.59 crore) are fully provided [Report p98–99]. Loans to related parties of Rs 2,978.81 crore are provided as doubtful [Report p104–106].
- **Sofinter stake:** A new investor would acquire 90% for Euro 12 million. The Gammon group's maximum exit is Euro 34 million at a Euro 135 million exit value [Report p127]. The group also needs about Euro 14 million of fresh equity, with a shortfall undertaking from Nova Energy [Report p24]. The stake is fully provided on a prudent basis [Report p206].
- **Pledged shares:** Shares of subsidiaries and associates are pledged with lenders (13,89,63,414 shares in total) [Report p121]. The IDBI invocation of AJR Infra shares reversed a provision of Rs 6.51 crore [Report p125].
- **Claims:** Retained good claims of only Rs 10.00 crore [Report p67, p107].

**Liabilities that offset any settlement:**
- Overdue principal of Rs 4,053.90 crore [Report p75; p79] and interest default of Rs 2,820.26 crore [Report p80].
- Penal interest of Rs 911.54 crore, including Rs 519.78 crore from CFM ARC, is contingent and not provided [Report p67; p121].
- Right of recompense to CDR lenders of Rs 504.96 crore is disclosed as a contingent liability [Report p106].

## 5. Gaps and inconsistencies

- The excerpts do not give the OTS amount, the haircut percentage, or the investor's identity and commitment size. "Everstone" and an "alternate investor" are named without terms.
- The excerpts do not show the lenders' approval status or an agreed settlement quantum.
- Campo Puma Oriente exposure is stated as Rs 430.19 crore with full provision [Report p127], but elsewhere a provision of Rs 230.41 crore is disclosed [Report p172]. The discrepancy is unresolved in the excerpts.
- The Kaleshwaram project (balance Rs 681 crore) and the Kolkata Metro package (balance Rs 9.49 crore) are listed as ongoing contracts [Report p5]. The excerpts do not show how they would contribute cash to a settlement.

**Conclusion for the ARC:** Any settlement would rely on lender or ARC acceptance of a principal-only or haircut structure, realisation of contested arbitration awards, and an external investor. The company has no evidenced liquid resources to fund a settlement itself.

# Reliance on Board, Management and Internal Controls: Directors' Claims vs Auditors' Findings

**Short answer:** The excerpts give little basis for relying on the Company's compliance, oversight or internal controls as currently described. The directors' statements are mostly generic or procedural. The statutory auditor, the secretarial auditor (Pramod Shah & Associates) and the practising company secretary certifying governance all report material failures. Several of the directors' own statements are contradicted by the same report. The Board composition and some procedural points are corroborated, but the substantive picture is weak.

Source: *Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 Gammon India Limited.pdf*, cited below as [AR p.X].

## 1. Directors' claims vs. what the auditors found

| Area | What the directors/management say | What the auditors/PCS found |
|---|---|---|
| **Internal controls** | Controls are designed to give assurance on reliable reporting, statutory compliance and safeguarding of assets, but "implementation and effectiveness in certain areas are affected due to manpower and liquidity issues" [AR p.33]. | The statutory auditor cannot state that internal financial controls were adequate or operating effectively as at 31 March 2026. Causes are "severe manpower issues" and "liquidity issues"; test of transactions revealed control weaknesses [AR p.78]. Internal audit was "not adequate" for the Company's size and operations [AR p.78, p.75]. |
| **CEO assurance** | The CEO declares "the adequacy and effectiveness of the Company's internal controls for financial reporting" [AR p.62]. | This conflicts directly with the auditor's conclusion above [AR p.78]. For the consolidated accounts the auditor identified material weaknesses, including period-end reporting processes that "were also inadequate leading to errors in consolidation" [AR p.150]. The consolidated ICFR opinion is modified [AR p.146]. |
| **Statutory compliance** | Company "has delayed" some filings, but "has since regularized" them and "necessary internal controls have been strengthened" [AR p.28, p.31]. | The auditor says the Company "is defaulting on its statutory and regulatory obligations" [AR p.68] and "is not regular in depositing undisputed statutory dues" [AR p.73]. The secretarial auditor reports ROC e-form delays through FY 2025-26 [AR p.37, p.63]. |
| **Company Secretary gap** | CS vacancy 16 June to 5 December 2025 caused MGT-14 delays of "36 days and 52 days" [AR p.28]. | The secretarial audit table shows the two MGT-14s: one due 02/09/2025 filed 24/10/2025 (52 days late) and one due 19/10/2025 filed 25/10/2025 (6 days late) [AR p.39]. The second figure is not 36 days as stated. The excerpts do not explain the difference. |
| **Directors' Report / Accounts** | Company "inadvertently missed" a disclosure, the Maternity Benefit Act disclosure [AR p.28]. | Confirmed by the secretarial auditor [AR p.38]. |
| **Board compliance** | Board "periodically reviews compliance reports... Steps are taken by the Company to rectify instances of non-compliances" [AR p.51]. | The Company failed to finalise FY 2024-25 audited results on time (approved 2 August 2025), which the PCS flagged under Regulation 33 [AR p.31, p.38]. Oversight failures are not shown to have been rectified. |
| **Compliance with Corporate Governance** | Company "has complied with the mandatory requirements of Regulation 27" [AR p.59]. The compliance table marks the "Disqualification of Director" check as "Yes" [AR p.29-30, p.41]. | The same table records that the Company defaulted on NCD repayments for over a year and that four directors are disqualified under Section 164(2)(b). The "Yes" answer and the disqualification observation are internally inconsistent [AR p.41]. |
| **Director eligibility** | Board is "duly constituted" with no change in composition [AR p.38]. Independent directors have declared their independence [AR p.53]. | The PCS certificate names four directors as disqualified under Section 164(2)(b): Kashi Nath Chatterjee, Lily Bhushan, Mahendra Ujamshi Shah and Vishwas Madhusudan Joglekar [AR p.41, p.63, p.65]. The statutory auditor says that, based on written representations, "all the directors are disqualified... except two" [AR p.70]. These two statements do not match. Kashi Nath Chatterjee and Mahendra Shah are on the Audit Committee [AR p.54]. |
| **Delisting / SAT directions** | Company "has complied with the directives of SAT" [AR p.28, p.38, p.63]. | The PCS notes that the Company has "complied to all compliance on BSE Portal till date" but "is in process to complete compliances with NSE" [AR p.63]. The NSE position is incomplete. The Company says it emailed NSE during portal unavailability [AR p.43]. |
| **Related parties / pecuniary interests** | No RPTs requiring AOC-2 disclosure; no omnibus approvals; no pecuniary relationships with directors or KMP beyond remuneration [AR p.33, p.52]. | The statutory auditor says that the director remuneration paid "was subject to No Objection Certificate to be received from the consortium of lenders... In the absence of NOC... not in accordance with... Section 197" [AR p.70]. The auditor also reports that all related-party transactions are compliant "in so far as our examination... is concerned" [AR p.75]. |
| **Board process** | Board meets at least quarterly; decisions are unanimous; systems exist to monitor compliance [AR p.51, p.38]. | The PCS confirms these procedural points [AR p.38]. However, the PCS's general opinion is limited: it did not verify the correctness of financial records and relied on the statutory auditor's report [AR p.39]. |

## 2. Points where the auditors support the directors

- The Board composition and procedures are corroborated by the secretarial auditor, who reports that the Board is properly constituted, decisions were unanimous and systems exist to monitor compliance [AR p.38].
- The PCS reports no SEBI or stock exchange actions against the Company, and no penalties under Regulation 33 for the previous three years [AR p.41-42, AR p.59].
- Board Secretarial Standards, policies, website and preservation of documents are reported as compliant [AR p.29-30, AR p.40-42].
- Audit trail (edit log) is enabled in the Tally system for the periods stated, though with gaps (see below).

These are mostly procedural and do not offset the substantive failures.

## 3. Other material oversight and control concerns from the auditors

- **Going concern:** Current liabilities exceed current assets by ₹12,701.41 crore. The auditor flags material uncertainty; the lenders' resolution plan has seen no progress [AR p.68].
- **Penal interest:** ₹391.76 crore of penal and incremental charges levied by lenders have not been debited to profit and loss and are disclosed as contingent liabilities [AR p.67].
- **Audit trail:** Tally's application-level edit log is retained only from 22 April 2024. For the later Tally Prime version, the audit trail is only available from 20 November 2025 [AR p.71, p.147]. Some subsidiaries' software has no audit trail at all [AR p.147].
- **Debenture Redemption Reserve:** No liquid assets of ₹43.25 crore set aside, as required, due to the financial crunch [AR p.86].
- **Internal audit:** Not commensurate with the size and nature of the business [AR p.75, p.78].

## 4. Limits of this evidence

- The excerpts do not include the full Board's explanations to each auditor qualification, the full Annexures, or the internal audit reports.
- The secretarial auditor expresses no view on financial records [AR p.39]. The PCS's governance certificate is "neither an assurance as to the future viability... nor of the efficiency or effectiveness" of management [AR p.63].
- The excerpt at AR p.43 contains an unfilled placeholder ("December [Year]"), so the portal-restoration date is unclear.
- The excerpts contain several unreconciled figures (for example, the 36-day MGT-14 delay and the disqualification count), which should be verified against the full filings before relying on them.

**Conclusion:** Reliance on the directors' statements about compliance, oversight and internal controls should be low. The auditors' reports contradict the directors on internal controls, the CEO's assurance, director eligibility and filing compliance. The Board's procedural statements are partly supported. Any decision should rest on the auditors' findings, not on the directors' general assurances.

answer:
**Short answer:** The excerpts do not support the headline claim. The management statement that the Company is "net cash positive as on Mar'26" [Inox Wind_Annual Report FY 2026.pdf p50] is contradicted by the Group's own gearing note, which reports net debt of ₹1,88,602.68 lakh. The phrase "free of interest-bearing debt" does not appear in the excerpts, and the notes show substantial interest-bearing borrowings. All figures below are in ₹ lakh unless stated.

**1. The headline claim**

- Management says the Company "continues to remain net cash positive as on Mar'26" [Inox Wind_Annual Report FY 2026.pdf p50]. The same page refers to the substation demerger into Inox Renewable Solutions Limited, which it describes as approved by NCLT Ahmedabad [p50]. The excerpts do not show any balance-sheet effect of that demerger.
- The Group's capital management note defines net debt as interest-bearing borrowings, payables and other items, less cash [p318]. Its table shows:
  - Total debt: 2,01,684.11 (2026) vs 1,51,837.15 (2025)
  - Cash and bank balances (excluding lien deposits): 13,081.43 vs 2,100.99
  - **Net debt: 1,88,602.68 (2026) vs 1,49,736.16 (2025)**
  - Net debt to equity: 29.55% vs 33.93% [p318]

**2. Reconciliation of borrowings (consolidated)**

| Item | 31-Mar-26 | 31-Mar-25 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Current borrowings (total) | 1,27,640.03 | 1,43,822.57 | p314 |
| Non-current borrowings | 27,506.89 | 190.04 | p318 / p323 |
| Total borrowings (contractual) | 1,55,146.92 | 1,44,012.61 | p323 |
| Cash and bank balances (amortised cost) | 61,205.90 | 21,331.50 | p318 |

Even using the larger cash figure of 61,205.90, borrowings of 1,55,146.92 leave a net debt of about 93,941. Using the gearing note's cash figure, net debt is 1,88,602.68. Neither basis yields net cash.

Within current borrowings (consolidated, p313–p314):
- Supplier credit: 55,850.13 (vs 24,134.01)
- Working capital demand loans: 39,000.00 (vs 13,400.00)
- Cash credit: 4,665.00 (vs 697.34)
- Overdraft: 16,810.57 (vs 16,668.48)
- Term loan: 2,000.00 (vs 2,000.00)
- Other financial institution loans: 3,100.00 (vs 17,947.83)
- Current maturities of non-current borrowings: 5,412.96 (vs 13,008.73)

Non-current borrowings rose sharply to 27,506.89, including secured term loans from Axis Finance (12,500), Jio Credit (10,000) and Piramal Finance (10,000), all at roughly 10–10.5% interest. These carry shortfall undertakings from Inox Wind Limited [p343–p345].

**3. Interest-bearing character of the debt**

The notes state interest rates on most of the borrowings:
- Inter-corporate deposits from related parties: 7%–12% [p313–p314]
- NCDs: 10.00% and 10.75% [p343]
- Working capital demand loans: 7.50%–11.20% [p345]
- Supplier credit facilities: benchmark (SOFR/EURIBOR) plus a bank spread of 0.30%–1.50%, and 0.40%–0.80% for a second facility [p345]

The only nil-interest item identified is a director loan of 45.08 [p314].

**4. Supplier financing**

- Supplier credit is classified as a bank borrowing, not as trade payables. Standalone supplier credit is 45,540.20 [p222]; consolidated is 55,850.13 [p313].
- The Ind AS 107 supplier-finance disclosure shows a carrying amount of 41,012.71 (vs 2,621.93), interest of 6.75%–8.06%, and payment terms of 0–180 days [p313]. The same 41,012.71 appears as "Payable to TReDs" in the gearing and liquidity tables [p318, p323].
- Because supplier finance is interest-bearing, it cannot be treated as free of interest-bearing debt.

**5. Working capital**

- Trade receivables increased to 4,24,983.90 (from 2,54,859.78) [p318].
- Consolidated trade payables increased to 1,18,911.76 (from 1,06,537.36) [p314].
- Advances from customers rose to 64,526.47 (from 30,233.10) [p313]. Customer advances partly fund the business, but they are not borrowings in the notes.
- Working capital is therefore funded substantially by supplier credit, working-capital loans and TReDs-linked payables, all of which are interest-bearing.

**6. Gaps and inconsistencies**

- The standalone net-cash position cannot be tested: the excerpts give standalone current borrowings (95,740.68 after interest accrued [p259]) but not standalone cash or non-current borrowings.
- The consolidated financing-liabilities table gives closing balances of 1,33,506.27 (current) and 32,938.28 (non-current) [p281], which do not match the balance-sheet notes (1,27,640.03 and 27,506.89). The excerpts do not reconcile the difference.
- The gearing note says net debt includes "trade and other payables," but the table's total debt does not appear to include trade payables of 1,18,911.76. The method is therefore not fully explained.
- The NCPRPS of 56,000 shown in 2025 falls to nil in 2026 [p314, p259]. The excerpts do not explain how it was settled.
- The p50 excerpt carries a footer reading "Annual Report 2024-25" [p50], although the document is labelled FY 2026. This should be checked against the source.

**Conclusion:** The notes contradict the net-cash claim. On the Group's own gearing definition, the balance sheet shows net debt, not net cash. Borrowings are interest-bearing, supplier finance is classified as bank borrowing, and working capital is financed largely by these facilities.

# Inox Wind's entanglement with its promoter group and subsidiaries, and what it means for a lender

Source for all citations: *Inox Wind Annual Report FY 2026* (cited as "AR p.X"). Figures are in ₹ Crore unless stated. Where I convert lakhs to crore (1 crore = 100 lakhs), I say so.

## 1. Orders and trading flows

- **Inox Green Energy Services Ltd (IGESL):** Inox Wind holds 51.13% and IGESL is a material subsidiary [AR p.106]. Inter-company dealings in the last financial year totalled ₹289.29 Cr, including ₹85.93 Cr of inter-corporate deposits (ICDs) given and ₹160.51 Cr received [AR p.106]. In the current year to the prior quarter, the total was ₹297.21 Cr, including ₹205.60 Cr of customer advances for goods sold [AR p.107].
- **Inox Renewable Solutions Ltd (IRSL):** Inox Wind holds 87.73% [AR p.113]. Last-year dealings totalled ₹1,148.80 Cr, including ₹574.51 Cr of ICDs given/received back, ₹220.50 Cr of sales and ₹155.17 Cr of purchases [AR p.113].
- **Inox Clean Energy Ltd (ICEL):** A group entity with no shareholding either way [AR p.122]. Last-year dealings totalled ₹623.17 Cr, including ₹387.15 Cr of customer advances and ₹224.36 Cr of sales [AR p.122].
- **Shri Devansh Jain (Whole-time Director, Promoter Director):** Holds 44.18% of the equity directly and through relatives and controlled entities [AR p.89].

## 2. Proposed enabling limits (shareholder approval sought)

- **IRSL:** ₹4,400 Cr in total, comprising ₹1,500 Cr of ICDs given, ₹1,500 Cr of ICDs received, ₹500 Cr of guarantees/securities, ₹600 Cr of sales and ₹100 Cr of purchases [AR p.114]. This is 100.06% of Inox Wind's consolidated turnover and 758.08% of IRSL's turnover [AR p.114].
- **IGESL:** ₹1,750 Cr, equal to 39.80% of Inox Wind's consolidated turnover and 622.75% of IGESL's consolidated turnover [AR p.107].
- **ICEL:** ₹500 Cr, equal to 11.37% of consolidated turnover [AR p.122].
- **Promoter Director loans:** Up to ₹600 Cr of loans from Shri Devansh Jain, with no previous loans in FY2025-26 [AR p.89–90]. Terms, including security, are "to be determined on an arm's length basis" [AR p.90].

The limits are described as enabling, and actual use "may be lower" [AR p.107, p.114].

## 3. Guarantees and commitments

- As at 31 March 2026, Inox Wind had a corporate guarantee of ₹18,050 lakhs (≈₹180.5 Cr) to a bank for a loan to ICEL [AR p.238, p.251].
- It had a guarantee of ₹2,915.87 lakhs (≈₹29.2 Cr) for IGESL facilities [AR p.238].
- It had a board-resolution "shortfall undertaking" against IRSL's financial-institution borrowings of ₹32,500 lakhs (≈₹325 Cr) [AR p.238]. The prior year figure was nil [AR p.238].
- As at 30 June 2026, guarantees for IGESL facilities were stated as ₹135 Cr [AR p.71]. This does not reconcile with the 31 March 2026 figure of ≈₹29.2 Cr; the excerpts do not explain the difference.

## 4. Funding exposure

- **ICD to IRSL:** ₹57,393.14 lakhs (≈₹573.9 Cr) outstanding at 31 March 2026, against a maximum balance of ₹70,391.61 lakhs during the year [AR p.286]. The prior year balance was nil [AR p.286].
- **ICD to IGESL:** Nil at 31 March 2026, against ₹9,870.98 lakhs at 31 March 2025 [AR p.286].
- **Circular flows:** In FY2025-26, ₹16,050.57 lakhs was received from IGESL and passed on to IRSL [AR p.295]. In FY2024-25, IRSL passed ₹20,961.29 lakhs to IGESL and ₹19,660.71 lakhs to IGREL Renewables, and IGESL passed ₹18,493.90 lakhs to IRSL [AR p.295].
- **Terms:** These ICDs are unsecured, repayable on demand, and carry 7.50%–12% p.a. [AR p.287].
- **Impairment history:** No expense was recognised for doubtful related-party ICDs in FY2025-26, against ₹1,346 lakhs in FY2024-25 [AR p.274].

## 5. Settlement and default position

- Related-party amounts outstanding are unsecured and "will be settled in cash or receipts of goods and services." No guarantees are held against related-party receivables or payables [AR p.238].
- The company reports no defaults by IGESL, IRSL or ICEL on obligations to Inox Wind [AR p.71, p.113, p.122].
- IGESL is reported as not classified as an NPA, not a wilful defaulter, and not in insolvency proceedings [AR p.76].
- IRSL is reported to have had no borrowing default and to have continued as a going concern [AR p.120]. Its CARE ratings are "CARE A / Stable" (long-term) and "CARE A1" (short-term) [AR p.120].
- Financial position: IRSL reported a standalone loss after tax of ₹55.44 Cr and a net worth of ₹1,430.25 Cr [AR p.114]. IGESL reported a standalone profit after tax of ₹52.47 Cr and a net worth of ₹1,731.51 Cr [AR p.107].

## 6. What this means for a lender to Inox Wind

1. **Large, mostly unsecured exposure to related parties.** Inox Wind's balance sheet carries about ₹574 Cr of ICDs to IRSL (unsecured, on demand) and contingent exposure of roughly ₹535 Cr from guarantees and the IRSL shortfall undertaking, based on the 31 March 2026 figures. A lender's repayment capacity therefore depends partly on whether IRSL and ICEL can repay or refinance.
2. **IRSL is the key concentration.** IRSL carries the largest ICD balance, the largest guarantee-type commitment (the ₹325 Cr shortfall undertaking) and a loss-making result. Its ₹4,400 Cr proposed limit is the largest in the approvals.
3. **Circular and promoter funding.** Funds move between group entities, and Inox Wind relies on loans from its promoter director (up to ₹600 Cr proposed). The excerpts do not show how these loans are secured or ranked.
4. **Inox Wind's own secured creditors rank first on its assets.** Its working capital demand loans (₹39,000 lakhs ≈ ₹390 Cr) and supplier's credit (₹45,380.35 lakhs ≈ ₹453.8 Cr) have first pari-passu charges on current and movable fixed assets, and second charges on the Rohika Plant [AR p.287]. Any lender to the parent would rank alongside or behind these secured facilities, and related-party receivables are unsecured.
5. **Limits are not usage.** The approved limits are ceilings, not actual usage, so the current exposure could be lower or could rise to the approved limits.

**Information gaps:** The excerpts do not give Inox Wind's own consolidated net worth, total debt, or cash flow, so I cannot assess leverage or debt-service capacity. They also do not explain the ₹135 Cr vs ₹29.2 Cr guarantee discrepancy, or the ranking of the promoter loans.

## Summary

The excerpts show that CEAT's debt rose substantially in FY2025-26, driven by the CAMSO acquisition, capex and subsidiary funding. Gearing, debt-to-EBITDA and interest coverage moved in a way the company describes as well-calibrated, and both rating agencies reaffirmed their ratings with a Positive outlook. The excerpts do not give the agencies' detailed reasoning beyond the points noted below.

## What changed

**Acquisition and capex**
- The CAMSO off-highway tyres and tracks business was acquired effective 1 September 2025 [CEATIntegratedAnnualReport2526Re.pdf p46; p87].
- Cash paid for the business combination was Rs 23,933 lakhs [p95]. CAMSO IP was the largest intangible addition, at about Rs 23,600 lakhs [p41].
- A separate binding commitment of USD 44 million for the CAMSO brand is payable after three years from acquisition [p123].
- Capex was about Rs 1,315 crore [p18], or Rs 1,31,531 lakhs [p45]. Cash outflow on PPE and intangibles was Rs 1,07,598 lakhs [p95].
- Contracted but unprovided capital commitments rose to Rs 1,78,488 lakhs from Rs 70,616 lakhs [p123].
- A loan of Rs 75,868 lakhs to CEAT OHT Lanka, a wholly owned subsidiary, carries 8% interest, with principal repayable from 31 December 2029 to 30 September 2035 [p42; p110].

**Leverage**
- Consolidated gross debt rose to Rs 3,01,079 lakhs from Rs 1,92,835 lakhs [p45]. Note that p173 shows the prior-year figure as Rs 1,92,908 lakhs.
- Net debt rose to Rs 2,96,110 lakhs from Rs 1,88,882 lakhs. Gearing rose to 37% from 31% [p130].
- Standalone debt-equity rose to 0.59 from 0.45 [p44]. Consolidated debt-equity is 0.60 [p188].
- Debt-to-EBITDA is about 1.46x [p45; p188].
- About 47% of borrowings are at fixed rates, up from 45% [p128].

**Liquidity**
- The current ratio was unchanged at 0.65 [p44].
- Standalone cash and cash equivalents at year-end were Rs 3,090 lakhs, down from Rs 3,947 lakhs [p95].
- Net cash from operating activities rose to Rs 1,83,989 lakhs from Rs 1,08,298 lakhs [p95].
- Working capital borrowings increased. Cash credit was Rs 11,991 lakhs (nil previously), and working capital demand loans were Rs 42,304 lakhs (Rs 13,000 lakhs previously) [p160].
- The company has a commercial paper limit of Rs 1,00,000 lakhs [p116].
- The cash conversion cycle is about (-3.8) days [p18].
- Cash flow is monitored daily [p129].

**Debt servicing**
- Standalone EBITDA rose about 37% to Rs 2,04,237 lakhs. Consolidated EBITDA rose 38% to Rs 2,06,300 lakhs [p45].
- Interest coverage improved to 5.17x from 4.90x [p44].
- Finance costs rose to Rs 35,947 lakhs from Rs 27,720 lakhs [p94]. Interest paid rose to Rs 31,288 lakhs from Rs 24,403 lakhs [p95].
- Standalone net profit rose to Rs 81,272 lakhs from Rs 48,210 lakhs [p94].
- Current maturities of long-term borrowings are Rs 46,981 lakhs [p112].
- Consolidated borrowings due in under one year are Rs 1,50,712 lakhs, and borrowings due in one to five years are Rs 1,49,878 lakhs in total liabilities [p175].
- Debt issuance and repayment: the Rs 100 crore 7.00% NCD was redeemed in October 2025, and a Rs 250 crore 7.20% NCD was issued in December 2025 and is due in 2030 [p59]. The Rs 150 crore 7.99% NCD is due 19 September 2026 [p59].
- New term loans of Rs 40,000 lakhs each from State Bank of India and Axis Bank are secured on Chennai plant movable assets [p113].
- The company reports no covenant breaches [p130].

## Rating agencies

- CARE reaffirmed the long-term rating at AA with a Positive outlook, extended it to proposed NCDs, and reaffirmed short-term and CP ratings at A1+ [p61].
- India Ratings (Ind-Ra) affirmed AA with a Positive outlook and assigned the same rating to proposed borrowings. CP limits were reaffirmed at A1+ [p61].
- CARE's reaffirmation considered the increase in long-term debt to fund ongoing expansions and the CAMSO acquisition [p61].

The excerpts do not contain the agencies' full rationale, such as detailed sensitivity analysis or their views on the CAMSO integration.

## Gaps

- The excerpts do not give the total purchase price for CAMSO, only the cash paid and the USD 44 million commitment.
- Figures for capex and debt differ slightly across sections, depending on basis (standalone or consolidated, and whether the figure includes intangibles or lease items). This answer cites the source for each figure.

**Short answer:** The excerpts point mainly to a business-model feature, not an acute liquidity problem. CEAT's current liabilities exceed current assets largely because suppliers, dealers and short-term bank lines fund operations. The risk is real but manageable: the company relies on rolling short-term and commercial paper funding, and its borrowings and near-term repayments have risen sharply. The excerpts do not give total current assets or total current liabilities, so I cannot reconcile the current ratio from first principles.

**1. Working-capital evidence (supports the business-model view)**
- The current ratio was 0.65 in both FY2025-26 and FY2024-25 [CEAT Integrated Annual Report p44], so the position is structural rather than newly deteriorating.
- The company reports a negative cash conversion cycle of about (-3.8) days [CEAT Integrated Annual Report p18], and states "Net working capital is negative" [CEAT Integrated Annual Report p132].
- Trade payable days rose to 98 from 90 [CEAT Integrated Annual Report p42]. Trade payables are non-interest bearing and normally settled over 30 to 180 days [CEAT Integrated Annual Report p117].
- Supplier-finance arrangements at 31 March 2026 included ₹49,317 lakhs presented as supplier's credit at 180 days after invoice date [CEAT Integrated Annual Report p161].
- Dealer deposits of ₹64,545 lakhs are current and payable on demand [CEAT Integrated Annual Report p129]. These are a significant non-bank funding source within current liabilities.

**2. Cash-flow evidence (supports the view that operations generate cash)**
- Cash flow from operations was ₹1,786 crore [CEAT Integrated Annual Report p18].
- Standalone net cash from operating activities was ₹1,83,989 lakhs, up from ₹1,08,298 lakhs. This reflects a ₹55,822 lakh increase in trade payables [CEAT Integrated Annual Report p95].

**3. Funding and risk evidence (points to genuine exposure)**
- Consolidated gross debt rose to ₹3,01,079 lakhs from ₹1,92,835 lakhs [CEAT Integrated Annual Report p45]. Debt-to-EBITDA is about 1.46x [CEAT Integrated Annual Report p45], and gearing rose to 37% from 31% [CEAT Integrated Annual Report p130].
- Short-term funding has grown. Working capital demand loans rose to ₹42,304 lakhs from ₹13,000 lakhs, and cash credit was ₹11,991 lakhs [CEAT Integrated Annual Report p160]. Standalone short-term borrowings were ₹1,01,852 lakhs at year-end [CEAT Integrated Annual Report p95]. Commercial paper has a total limit of ₹1,00,000 lakhs [CEAT Integrated Annual Report p116].
- Current maturities of long-term borrowings were ₹46,981 lakhs [CEAT Integrated Annual Report p157], and current borrowings with contractual maturity under one year were ₹1,48,833 lakhs [CEAT Integrated Annual Report p129].
- Cash and cash equivalents were only ₹3,090 lakhs [CEAT Integrated Annual Report p95]. The company says any shortfall is funded by short-term loans [CEAT Integrated Annual Report p129]. This means liquidity depends on continued access to bank and CP funding.
- Net financing inflow was ₹46,950 lakhs, compared with an outflow of ₹(14,022) lakhs the prior year [CEAT Integrated Annual Report p44]. This was driven by new borrowings while the company invested heavily. Capex was about ₹1,315 crore [CEAT Integrated Annual Report p18], and loans to a subsidiary were ₹70,154 lakhs [CEAT Integrated Annual Report p44].
- Mitigants: CARE rated the long-term debt AA (Positive) and short-term facilities A1+ [CEAT Integrated Annual Report p61]. The auditor reported no material uncertainty about meeting liabilities falling due within one year, though this is expressly not an assurance of future viability [CEAT Integrated Annual Report p92].

**Conclusion:** The negative working capital and current ratio below 1 are consistent with a business that collects cash quickly, holds dealer deposits, and uses supplier credit. Operating cash flow is strong and the ratings are high. The genuine risk is the rising reliance on short-term and rolled-over funding alongside large capex, acquisition-related outflows and near-term debt maturities. If bank or CP access tightened, or payables were shortened, the company would need to rely on its cash generation and existing facilities. The excerpts do not show a liquidity shortfall.

### 1. What Refex has exited

### 2. What Refex is leaning into

- **Ash & coal handling:** This is described as the Group's largest vertical. The company services more than 40 thermal power plants across 15+ states [PDF p54]. Its 2025 entry was described as a move to scale up the high-margin ash handling business [PDF p7].

- **Premium corporate mobility (Refex Green Mobility):** Mobility revenue rose 164%, from ₹38 crore to ₹100 crore [PDF p57].

### 3. How the shift changes the risk profile of revenue

- **Concentration remains high.** In FY 2025-26, Ash & Coal was 83.46% of revenue, Wind 9.85%, Mobility 4.13% and Others 2.56%. This is on a consolidated basis, covering both continuing and discontinued operations [PDF p15]. Ash & Coal is still the dominant exposure to thermal power customers.

- **Non-interest-bearing share** of total deposits fell to 42.5%, down 4 ppts [p52].
- **Composition** (SAR bn, 2025 vs 2024) [p317]:

- Within the time deposits, SAR 96.6bn of SAR 111.3bn falls due within 3 months [p355]. This is a short-tenor, rate-sensitive base.

### 2. Wholesale and non-deposit funding
- **Interbank and central bank funding fell sharply.** Due to SAMA fell to SAR 5.0bn from 12.5bn, and due to banks and FIs fell to SAR 7.9bn from 19.8bn [p267].
- **Debt securities and term loans** rose 151% to SAR 38.9bn from 15.5bn, driven by multiple issuances [p51, p267]. Management says BSF "tactically shifted toward non-deposit funding" because deposit growth lagged loan growth, amid stiff competition for deposits [p70].

The debt schedule also lists a SAR 1.5bn bilateral loan (March), a USD 1bn syndicated loan (July), a USD 1bn Tier II bond (September) and a USD 750m syndicated loan (October) [p208].

- The Group reports diversifying funding through capital markets, with traction in Far East markets [p28, p70].

### 4. Overall assessment
- **Trajectory:** Liquidity conditions tightened and funding costs rose during 2025 [p28]. Funding costs increased 4% to SAR 8.9bn [p51]. The bank nonetheless moved from interbank and SAMA borrowing toward term capital-market funding and reduced its loan-to-deposit ratio.
- **Versus a year ago, on the reported metrics:** the position is stronger. LCR, NSFR and the weighted loan-to-deposit ratio all improved.
- **Qualitative caveats (my inference, not stated in the report):** the deposit base is less sticky. Non-interest-bearing funding fell, and most time deposits mature within three months. Funding is also more reliant on term debt and rate-sensitive deposits. The excerpts do not contain management's own statement that resilience has improved or weakened versus 2024.
- **Outlook:** BSF plans to focus funding on CASA and other stable sources, prioritise capital-light lending, and use treasury to optimise funding costs [p36].

**Short answer:** Yes, on most measures the loan book is getting riskier. The fall in the impairment charge does not reflect better asset quality. It is mainly due to larger recoveries. Problem loans rose faster than the book, coverage fell, and the gross credit-loss charge increased. Figures marked "calc." are my calculations from the excerpted tables.

**1. Growth mix: faster growth in consumer lending, with the riskier segments growing fastest**
- Loans and advances rose 5% YoY to SAR 214.9bn. Consumer loans rose 18%, driven by mortgages (+24%) and personal loans (+12%). Commercial loans rose only 2%, with services up and commerce, contracting and manufacturing down [BSF-2025 Integrated Annual Report p51].
- Gross loans were SAR 218.7bn versus SAR 207.7bn [BSF-2025 Integrated Annual Report p304].
- Calc.: Consumer loans went from about 18.0% to 20.1% of the gross book. Overdraft and commercial loans fell from about 81.7% to 79.4%.
- Credit cards grew about 33% (SAR 0.996bn vs 0.749bn) and auto lease about 11% [BSF-2025 Integrated Annual Report p305]. Credit cards carry the highest NPL ratio in the book (see below).

**2. Problem loans: rising in absolute terms and as a share of the book**
- Net non-performing loans (NPLs) rose to SAR 2.12bn from SAR 1.93bn, up about 9.5% (calc.) [BSF-2025 Integrated Annual Report p304, p338].
- The NPL ratio rose to 0.97%, up 4 bps, "reflecting higher NPLs in both commercial and consumer portfolios" [BSF-2025 Integrated Annual Report p51–52].
- Calc. by segment, using the net NPL and gross loan figures:
  - Overdraft and commercial: about 0.99% vs 0.97%.
  - Consumer: about 0.81% vs 0.73%.
  - Credit cards: about 3.8% vs 3.3%.
- Stage 3 (lifetime ECL, credit-impaired) gross balances rose about 21% to SAR 2.53bn from SAR 2.09bn. As a share of gross loans, that is about 1.16% vs 1.01% (calc.) [BSF-2025 Integrated Annual Report p306].
- Stage 2 (lifetime ECL, not credit-impaired) rose about 9% to SAR 12.8bn, from about 5.6% to 5.9% of the book (calc.) [BSF-2025 Integrated Annual Report p306].
- Special-mention exposures in aggregate fell slightly to SAR 3.30bn from SAR 3.39bn [BSF-2025 Integrated Annual Report p338]. This is a partial offset, though the excerpt does not explain the change.

**3. Coverage: weaker, though still high**
- The NPL coverage ratio fell 3.3 ppts to 178.4% [BSF-2025 Integrated Annual Report p51–52]. Total allowance of SAR 3.78bn against net NPLs of SAR 2.12bn reproduces this figure (calc.). The prior-year ratio would have been about 181.7%.
- Stage 3 allowance coverage rose to about 70.5% from about 63.3% (calc.: SAR 1.79bn against SAR 2.53bn), with the allowance on commercial stage 3 rising 34% [BSF-2025 Integrated Annual Report p306, p308, p338]. Because the stage 3 balance also grew, the coverage rise does not offset the NPL ratio increase.
- Total allowance rose to about 1.73% of gross loans from about 1.69% (calc.).

**4. Provisioning: the charge fell only because of recoveries**
- The net impairment charge on loans fell to SAR 974m from SAR 1,144m [BSF-2025 Integrated Annual Report p268].
- Gross ECL charge on loans rose about 7%, to SAR 1,381m from SAR 1,288m. Recoveries of written-off loans increased sharply, to SAR 407m from SAR 144m [BSF-2025 Integrated Annual Report p309].
- The bank attributes the lower total charge to "lower commercial loans, investment, and other impairments," with the SAR 407m recovery "partially offset by an increase in consumer impairments" [BSF-2025 Integrated Annual Report p51].
- Cost of risk fell 13 bps to 0.45% [BSF-2025 Integrated Annual Report p52]. This is the headline improvement, but it is flattered by recoveries.
- Write-offs in the excerpted tables are not cleanly split by product. One table shows SAR 1,116m against SAR 417m in the prior year, but its labelling is inconsistent, so I have not relied on it.

**Conclusion:** The bank's cost of risk and charge both fell, but this is mostly from higher recoveries. Gross provisioning rose, NPLs grew faster than loans, and stage 3 and stage 2 balances increased. Consumer and credit-card books are deteriorating from a low base, while commercial asset quality is weakening modestly. Coverage is still high, at 178%, and the NPL ratio of 0.97% remains low. On the evidence in these excerpts, the book is riskier, but the rise is moderate rather than severe.

- Other reserves rose from SAR (0.60)bn to SAR 0.75bn, mainly from FVOCI and cash-flow hedge movements. [BSF-2025 p320]
- The Board report and Financial Review attribute the growth to retained earnings, the USD 650m AT1 issuance in Q2 2025, the SAR 2.5bn Q4 2025 Tier I issuance, partly offset by the SAR 5bn redemption. [BSF-2025 p51; p209]

**Reliance on hybrid and subordinated instruments**

- **AT1 (hybrid):** Net contribution is negative. Gross AT1 issuance of about SAR 4.94bn was more than offset by the SAR 5.0bn call. AT1 fell by SAR 62.5m and its share of RWA fell from about 3.17% to 3.01%, a drag of roughly −0.16 ppts on the Tier I + II ratio. [BSF-2025 p209; p363]
- **Tier II (subordinated):** This is the largest driver of the ratio gain. Tier II rose by SAR 3.56bn, which accounts for about 55% of the SAR 6.51bn increase in Tier I + II capital and about +1.3 ppts of the 1.59 ppt ratio gain. The excerpts do not identify which instruments make up Tier II, so I cannot say how much is subordinated debt versus other items. [BSF-2025 p363]
- **CET1 (retained earnings and reserves):** CET1 added SAR 3.02bn, about 46% of the capital increase and about +0.45 ppts of the ratio. The excerpts do not provide a bridge from book equity to CET1, so the split between retained earnings and other reserves within CET1 cannot be quantified.

In short, roughly 55% of the capital increase (and most of the ratio gain) comes from Tier II. About 46% comes from CET1, and AT1 hybrids net to slightly negative. Retained-earnings-driven CET1 is therefore a smaller share of the ratio improvement than the headline Tier I + II figure suggests.

## Inconsistencies and presentation issues

1. **CET1 exceeds book equity.** CET1 (SAR 42.76bn) is higher than equity attributable to shareholders (SAR 42.72bn) at end-2025, and the same pattern holds in 2024 (39.75bn vs 39.14bn). Regulatory deductions would normally reduce CET1 below book equity, and the excerpts do not show the adjustments. [BSF-2025 p267; p363]
2. **Tier I labels vary.** The KPI page uses "T1 ratio 19.2%, up 0.3 ppts", while Note 39 uses "Tier I ratio 19.21%" (+0.29 ppts). The rounding is consistent, but the terminology is not. [BSF-2025 p52; p363]
3. **Note numbering is out of order.** "Capital Adequacy" is labelled Note 40 and appears before "Capital risk management", labelled Note 39, on the same page. The RWA and ratio table sits under the Note 39 heading. [BSF-2025 p363]
4. **Equity growth is rounded.** The Financial Review says total equity rose "7%", but the statements show about 7.5% (47.14bn to 50.66bn). [BSF-2025 p51; p267]
5. **2024 comparatives are restated.** Equity, RWA, and capital figures for 2024 are marked as restated, and the 2024 opening equity was adjusted by SAR 531m for prior-year impacts. Year-on-year ratio changes therefore compare restated figures with restated figures. [BSF-2025 p270; p271; p363]
6. **Capital narrative omits the Tier II driver.** The Financial Review explains the equity movement, but it does not mention the SAR 3.56bn Tier II increase that drives most of the ratio gain. [BSF-2025 p51; p363]

## Answer: Aldar's leverage and liquidity, 2024 vs 2023

**Short answer:** Leverage has genuinely improved on the reported metric, but the improvement is partly flattered by cash, and by a large fall in net payables that is not explained in the excerpts. Gross borrowings rose. Some of the cash is customer escrow money, so headline liquidity overstates what Aldar can freely deploy. Operating cash flow is not in the excerpts, so the cash build cannot be traced to its source.

### 1. Leverage (EPRA LTV)

- EPRA LTV fell to 12.0% from 17.5% [aldar_annual_report_2024.pdf p130; p135]. On the Group column it fell from 24.0% to 12.0%, and on the Combined column from 17.5% to 9.8% [p135].
- Management attributes the decrease "mainly" to "the increase in cash and properties held for sale" [p135].
- The table shows two offsetting movements on the Group basis:
  - **Gross debt rose.** Borrowings from financial institutions went from AED 6.58bn to 9.53bn, and bond loans from AED 5.50bn to 6.86bn. Hybrids were flat at AED 1.82bn [p135].
  - **Net payables fell sharply.** Group net payables went from AED 11.68bn to 5.21bn [p135]. This is a larger driver than the reported explanation implies. Net payables are inside the net debt calculation, so their fall reduces measured leverage.
- Net debt (Group) fell from AED 13.86bn to 8.27bn. Cash, which is deducted, rose from AED 11.72bn to 15.14bn [p135]. The denominator, total property value, also rose from AED 57.7bn to 69.2bn [p135].
- Aldar's own policy limits are leverage below 25% for Development and below 40% for Investment [p291]. Segment-level leverage is not in the excerpts.

### 2. Quality of the cash on hand

- Cash and bank balances rose to AED 15.14bn from 11.72bn [p196].
- Cash and cash equivalents, on the cash-flow definition (net of restricted balances and deposits over three months), rose to AED 10.22bn from 4.96bn [p271; p203].
- Restricted bank balances fell to AED 4.69bn from 6.64bn [p271].
- Within cash and cash equivalents, **AED 8,040,823k is escrow cash from customers** for development sales, which is available on demand but subject to performance bonds (2023: nil) [p271].
- A further AED 1.83bn is customer funding for specific projects, usable at the Company's discretion [p271]. The excerpts do not say whether this overlaps with the escrow figure.
- Derived: excluding the AED 8.04bn escrow balance, cash and cash equivalents would be about AED 2.2bn. This is my calculation, not a disclosed figure.
- Gross bank borrowings and sukuk total about AED 16.4bn [p304]. Book cash of AED 15.14bn therefore leaves net debt of about AED 1.25bn, against about AED 0.36bn in 2023. On the cash-flow definition, net debt is about AED 6.2bn against about AED 7.1bn in 2023 (derived from p304 and p203). Both are derived, and both depend on how much of the cash is treated as free.
- Net cash from operating activities is not in the excerpts, so the source of the AED 5.36bn net cash increase [p203] cannot be assessed. Financing inflows were AED 1.75bn, and bank borrowings drawn (AED 10.31bn) exceeded repayments (AED 7.19bn) [p202].

### 3. Debt structure

- **Bank borrowings:** AED 9.53bn in total, of which AED 0.62bn is current and AED 8.90bn non-current [p275].
- **Non-convertible sukuk:** AED 6.86bn in total, of which AED 1.43bn is current and AED 5.43bn non-current [p273].
- **Current debt:** about AED 2.05bn combined (derived).
- **Current sukuk:** AED 1.39bn of the current sukuk is Sukuk No. 1, due September 2025. Aldar redeemed USD 124.1m (AED 455.9m) early at a discount [p273]. It also initiated a buy-back of the September 2025 sukuk, funded by the new issuance and used to repay revolving facilities [p100].
- **Security:** most listed facilities are unsecured and general corporate purpose. The secured facilities in the loan table total about AED 275m (derived, 2024), mostly project finance [p275]. AIP repaid its three term loans for AED 1.2bn and all secured debt, leaving AIP with 100% unsecured debt [p100]. This applies to AIP, not the whole Group.
- **Cost and rate exposure:** the weighted average cost of debt rose to 5.55% from 5.15% [p291]. Finance costs on bank borrowings and sukuk rose to AED 873m from AED 584m [p285]. A 100 bp rate move would change net profit by AED 83.4m, up from AED 42.4m [p292].
- **Maturity profile:** financial liabilities by maturity show AED 8.9bn of bank borrowings in the 1–5 year bucket, and sukuk of AED 5.4bn beyond five years [p294].

### 4. Funding sources

- **Sukuk:** USD 500m, 10-year green sukuk at 5.5% coupon, at a 110 bp credit spread, four times oversubscribed, the tightest spread ever for AIP [p100; p178].
- **Committed bank facilities:** AED 4.0bn of new five-year committed revolvers signed with local banks, of which AED 3.19bn was drawn by year-end [p277].
- **Term loan:** GBP 325m (AED 1.50bn) unsecured term loan at an international subsidiary, refinanced and upsized, with a four-year maturity [p277].
- **Hybrids:** AED 1.82bn of hybrid equity from AIP's 2022 perpetual notes, with coupon payments of AED 103m [p272; p202].
- **Equity:** total equity rose to AED 42.8bn from 38.2bn [p197]. Equity as a share of total assets fell slightly, from about 52% to about 50% (derived).
- **Ratings:** Moody's rates AIP Baa1 with a stable outlook, affirmed in August [p100]. Aldar Properties is shown as Baa2 [p8]. The excerpts do not state an outlook for Aldar Properties.

### 5. Headroom

- **Undrawn facilities:** AED 8.11bn of undrawn committed term and revolving facilities at year-end, up from AED 7.47bn [p277]. This is the strongest headroom signal in the excerpts.
- **Post year-end:** Aldar Properties finalised a AED 9bn sustainability-linked five-year senior unsecured revolving facility on 10 January 2025 [p316]. It also issued USD 500m of resettable subordinated hybrid notes on 5 February 2025, at 7.0% [p316]. A further USD hybrid issue on 15 January 2025 is cited, but its amount is truncated in the excerpt [p316]. These are not reflected in the 2024 balance sheet. They add liquidity but also add hybrid and bank debt.
- **Covenants:** 18 borrowing arrangements carry minimum tangible net worth covenants. Two require AED 10bn, seven require AED 6bn and nine require AED 4bn [p292]. Equity attributable to owners was AED 34.9bn and EPRA NTA was AED 50.9bn [p197; p130]. The covenant definition of tangible net worth is not given, so headroom cannot be quantified.
- **Current ratio:** current assets of AED 46.9bn against current liabilities of AED 23.1bn gives about 2.03x. This was almost unchanged from 2023 (derived). Current liabilities are dominated by trade payables (AED 11.4bn) and income tax payable (AED 7.7bn), not by debt [p196; p198].

### 6. Gaps in the excerpts

- Net cash from operating activities, and so the cash conversion of earnings.
- Segment-level leverage against the 25% and 40% policy limits.
- Covenant definitions and actual headroom against the tangible net worth thresholds.
- Interest cover and EBITDA, needed to test debt service.
- Whether the AED 1.83bn project balance overlaps with the AED 8.04bn escrow balance.
- The full amount of the 15 January 2025 hybrid issue.

### Conclusion

Leverage has improved. The EPRA LTV decline is real on the reported definition, but it is driven by both higher cash and a large fall in net payables, while gross debt has risen by about AED 6.7bn [p135; p304]. Liquidity is stronger on a headline basis, but roughly 80% of the cash-and-equivalents balance is customer escrow, and about AED 2.2bn is available once that is excluded (derived). Headroom is supported by AED 8.1bn of undrawn facilities and the early-2025 funding. The excerpts do not allow a full judgement on sustainability without operating cash flow and covenant detail.

**Short answer:** Aldar's receivables are concentrated in a few large counterparties, and the share of receivables more than 180 days past due has risen sharply while the trade-receivable provision has fallen. The excerpts do not include management's own adequacy assessment or the ECL rates applied to each ageing bucket, so they cannot confirm whether provisioning is sufficient.

**1. Exposure to customers and counterparties**

- Net trade receivables were AED 5,404,232k in 2024 (2023: AED 5,272,867k), after an expected credit loss (ECL) allowance of AED 193,923k (2023: AED 234,634k) [aldar_annual_report_2024.pdf p264].
- Top five customers accounted for 6% of trade receivables in both 2024 and 2023 [aldar_annual_report_2024.pdf p264].
- Related-party and government balances are material. Trade and other receivables from the Government of Abu Dhabi were AED 1,028,304k (2023: AED 868,053k). Receivables from the parent company and its affiliates rose to AED 677,823k (2023: AED 100,334k) [aldar_annual_report_2024.pdf p288].
- The maximum credit exposure approximates carrying value [aldar_annual_report_2024.pdf p294]. Aldar holds no collateral except that receivables on property development are secured over the underlying units [aldar_annual_report_2024.pdf p294].
- Mitigants cited include instalment payments already received, some substantial, which Aldar could retain on non-completion [aldar_annual_report_2024.pdf p264, p293].

**2. Ageing of receivables**

|---|---|---|
| Not past due | 3,014,106 | 3,390,461 |
| Past due up to 180 days | 929,469 | 1,065,767 |

[aldar_annual_report_2024.pdf p265]

- The more-than-180-day bucket rose by about 79% year on year. Its share of the total went from about 15.5% to about 27.0% (my calculation).
- The not-past-due share fell from about 64% to about 56% (my calculation).
- The table is headed "non-impaired receivables" but totals to the net figure of AED 5,404,232k, so it is unclear whether the buckets are gross or net of ECL [aldar_annual_report_2024.pdf p265].

**3. Is provisioning keeping pace?**

- The trade-receivable ECL charge fell from AED 45,152k to AED 8,442k. Net write-offs of provisions rose from AED 20,029k to AED 49,153k. The closing allowance fell from AED 234,634k to AED 193,923k [aldar_annual_report_2024.pdf p266].
- Allowance coverage of gross trade receivables fell from about 4.3% to about 3.5% (my calculation from AED 5,507,501k and AED 5,598,155k gross) [aldar_annual_report_2024.pdf p264].
- Over the same period, the more-than-180-day balance grew by about AED 644m. The allowance fell by about AED 41m. Coverage of that bucket is only indicative, because the allowance covers the whole portfolio.
- Mitigating factors:
  - Default is presumed at more than 90 days past due unless there is information to the contrary [aldar_annual_report_2024.pdf p238].
  - Write-off occurs when balances are over two years past due or earlier if recovery is unlikely [aldar_annual_report_2024.pdf p240].
  - ECL rates are banded by counterparty category: government-related 0%, low-risk private 1–20%, high-risk private 20–60%, and defaulted 100% [aldar_annual_report_2024.pdf p266].
  - Management states that credit risk is "significantly reduced" [aldar_annual_report_2024.pdf p293].
- Government receivables: a table on p265, which follows the discussion of Government of Abu Dhabi receivables, shows gross balances of AED 270,849k non-current and AED 25,698k current, against ECL allowances of AED 215,155k and AED 24,857k. The table does not label the counterparty, and a 0% government ECL rate is stated for Category I [aldar_annual_report_2024.pdf p265, p266]. This needs clarification before drawing conclusions.

**Limits of the evidence**

The excerpts do not give ECL rates by ageing bucket, the sensitivity amounts for the ±5% scenario, or management's own adequacy conclusion. A firm view on whether provisioning is adequate would require those figures. On the evidence provided, the falling allowance and coverage, set against the sharp rise in long-dated receivables, suggest provisioning has not kept pace with ageing on this measure.

## Summary

The swing in debt-service metrics was driven almost entirely by finance costs, not by operating performance. Finance costs were abnormally high in FY2024-25 because of a one-time interest payment, and they fell back to a very low level in FY2025-26. Underlying operating earnings and cash generation weakened over the same period, so the headline improvement in debt-service coverage overstates any improvement in the company's underlying ability to service debt.

## What drove the swing

- **Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR):** 327.62x (FY2023-24) → 2.24x (FY2024-25) → 211.18x (FY2025-26) [FY2025 AR p105; FY2026 AR p110].
- **Finance cost:** ₹0.93 lakhs (FY2023-24), ₹237.41 lakhs (FY2024-25), ₹1.41 lakhs (FY2025-26) [FY2025 AR p36; FY2026 AR p6]. Of the FY2024-25 figure, interest was ₹234.60 lakhs and other borrowing cost ₹2.81 lakhs [FY2025 AR p101].
- **The FY2024-25 drop:** The prior-year report attributes the fall in DSCR and interest coverage to a "one time payment of interest cost to HSIIDC" [FY2025 AR p37].
- **The FY2025-26 rebound:** The current report attributes the rise to "reduction in Interest Cost" [FY2026 AR p38, p110].

In effect, FY2024-25 was the outlier. FY2025-26's finance cost (₹1.41 lakhs) is close to the FY2023-24 level (₹0.93 lakhs), which explains why the two years look similar in kind.

## Did underlying debt-servicing ability improve or weaken?

**Weaker on operating measures:**
- Revenue from operations fell from ₹16,025.02 to ₹14,897.55 lakhs [FY2026 AR p6].
- EBITDA margin fell from 3.78% to 2.53% [FY2026 AR p39].
- Operating profit before working-capital changes fell from ₹531.25 to ₹272.59 lakhs [FY2026 AR p90].
- EBIT (profit before tax plus finance cost) was about ₹320.10 lakhs in FY2025-26 versus ₹545.19 lakhs in FY2024-25, derived from [FY2026 AR p6] and [FY2025 AR p36]. Return on capital employed fell from 13.03% to 7.18%, attributed to lower pre-interest earnings [FY2026 AR p110].
- Net cash from operating activities turned negative at ₹(115.84) lakhs, compared with ₹569.06 lakhs in FY2024-25. The reported driver is a build-up in trade receivables (₹(674.56) lakhs) [FY2026 AR p90]. Trade receivables rose from ₹2,231.34 to ₹2,905.90 lakhs [FY2026 AR p88].

**Higher debt, though still low:**
- Total borrowings rose from ₹159.64 to ₹352.11 lakhs, and the debt-equity ratio rose from 0.04 to 0.08 [FY2026 AR p88, p110]. The company attributes this to increased debt [FY2026 AR p38].

**Stable on credit standing:**
- The company reports no defaults on interest or loan repayments [FY2026 AR p10].
- Acuité reaffirmed the long-term rating at 'ACUITE BBB' and the short-term rating at 'ACUITE A3+', with a 'Stable' outlook [FY2026 AR p10, p68].

## Limitations

- The DSCR denominator includes principal repayments, and the excerpts do not disclose principal repayment amounts or the numerator. The reported 211.18x therefore cannot be fully reconciled from the excerpts.
- The excerpts do not give the amount of the one-time HSIIDC payment separately.

## Conclusion

The DSCR swing reflects a one-time interest spike in FY2024-25 and a return to minimal finance costs in FY2025-26. It does not reflect a stronger earnings base. Underlying operating earnings, margins, and operating cash flow weakened in FY2025-26, and borrowings rose. Debt-servicing capacity remains comfortable given the low interest burden and reaffirmed credit rating, but the improvement in the headline ratio should not be read as an improvement in underlying ability to service debt.
